name: igraph
baseline: NetworkX 2.4 (pure Python); SNAP 5.0.0 as a second row
workload: Median wall time of graph loading, single-source shortest path, PageRank (damping 0.85, tol 1e-3), k-core and strongly connected components on the SNAP datasets amazon0302, web-Google and soc-Pokec, through the Python bindings (python-igraph 0.8.2 against networkx 2.4, Python 3.8).
claimed_speedup: Seconds for igraph vs NetworkX (Amazon / Google / Pokec): PageRank 0.57 / 2.42 / 23.39 vs 8.59 / 33.5 / 239.75 (about 15x / 14x / 10x, derived from page data); k-core 0.15 / 0.92 / 5.99 vs 3.63 / 42.6 / 296.26 (about 24x / 46x / 49x, derived); strongly connected components 0.22 / 1.38 / 3.96 vs 2.22 / 7.77 / 61.74 (about 10x / 5.6x / 16x, derived); shortest path 0.05 / 0.41 / 0.6 vs 1.37 / 3.41 / 5.65 (about 27x / 8x / 9x, derived); loading 0.57 / 3.87 / 25.75 vs 4.72 / 19.24 / 140.19 (about 8x / 5x / 5x, derived). Versus SNAP: loading 25.75 vs 52.73 s and shortest path 0.6 vs 2.3 s on Pokec.
compiler_and_flags: not stated; python-igraph 0.8.2 installed as a conda-forge binary (setup/setup.md), Python 3.8
hardware: Google Compute n1-standard-16 (16 vCPU Haswell 2.3 GHz, 60 GB); exact CPU model not given
stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars (igraph/igraph); widely used R, Python and Mathematica bindings
tradeoffs: GPL license (copyleft) limits embedding in permissive projects. The C core is called through wrappers (R, Python, Mathematica); the benchmark measures the Python binding, so interpreter overhead and type conversion are included.
caveats: Numbers are third-party (timlrx/graph-benchmarks, MIT repo, public profiling scripts in code/ and a run_profiler.sh driver) and live in the README image runtime_results.png; the linked blog post (timlrx.com) is egress-blocked here. The win is against pure-Python NetworkX, not a C or C++ library. In the same table igraph is slower than graph-tool, LightGraphs (Julia) and NetworKit on nearly every algorithm (Google PageRank 2.42 s vs 0.36 / 0.06 / 0.10 s; Pokec PageRank 23.39 s vs 1.1 / 0.21 / 0.24 s) and slower than SNAP on PageRank (Google 2.42 vs 2.31 s, Pokec 23.39 vs 8.62 s) and on Google shortest path (0.41 vs 0.26 s); only loading is faster than graph-tool and LightGraphs. Versions are from 2020 (igraph 0.8.2, networkx 2.4); igraph has changed since. NetworkX loading uses read_edgelist into a DiGraph. Compiler, flags and exact CPU model are not stated, hence tier B not A. Medians over 100 runs (Amazon, Google) or 10 runs (Pokec), NetworkX run fewer times. The category graph-algorithms is a suggestion: the guessed sequence-containers does not fit.

name: iguana (struct_pb)
workload: Monster message (game-monster struct with nested fields), serialize and deserialize loops of iguana::to_pb / from_pb against protobuf's generated code, in benchmark/pb_benchmark.cpp (bench3).
claimed_speedup: In the benchmark monster scenario struct_pb serialization is 2.4x protobuf and deserialization is 3.4x protobuf (README text lang/struct_pb_intro.md, translated from Chinese: 'serialization speed is 2.4 times protobuf, deserialization 3.4 times').
compiler_and_flags: CMake default build type Release with -O3 (CMakeLists.txt); compiler and version not stated for the claim
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17/C++20 (C++26 reflection path with GCC 16.1); structs defined in C++ with YLT_REFL / YLT_REFL_PB instead of .proto files and protoc. Protobuf support is proto3 binary wire only: no proto2 required fields, extensions, custom options or services, no proto3 JSON or text format; official conformance runs only the binary subset.
caveats: First-party claim in a Chinese-language doc; the numbers carry no hardware, compiler version or protobuf version, and the doc points to the struct_pack benchmark for reproduction. The in-repo benchmark/pb_benchmark.cpp prints iguana/protobuf ratios from a high_resolution_clock around whole loops (default 100000 iterations) but commits no results; deserialization allocates a fresh object per iteration for both libraries. The claim may predate the current code, which was refactored heavily (C++26 reflection, a new DOM parser PR #386 still open). The README FAQ answer 'Is iguana high performance? Yes, because it is based on compile-time reflection' has no numbers. No JSON-versus-RapidJSON or other numbers found in README or docs.

name: ICU (ICU4C collation)
baseline: glibc strcoll (glibc 2.12.3 in the ICU4C 3.8 chart, glibc 2.13 in the ICU4C 4.8 chart)
workload: String comparison (strcoll), sort key generation (keygen) and sort key length (keylen) of an ICU4C RuleBasedCollator with default options against glibc, over a large list of language-specific names, each operation repeated 1000 times, per locale.
claimed_speedup: en_US with Latin test data: strcoll 199%, keygen 77%, keylen 99% in ICU4C's favour (chart convention: positive means ICU4C better); ja_JP strcoll 421% in ICU4C's favour (snippet only, which chart not identified).
tradeoffs: Large library with its own data tables; UTF-16 is its native string form; ICU4C offers C and C++ APIs; Unicode-3.0 license (older releases used the ICU license).
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: icu.unicode.org, the PostgreSQL mailing list and lists.gnupg.org are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so the numbers come from WebSearch result text, not an opened page; percentages are chart deltas, not ratios, and the chart's platform, CPU and compiler fields were not readable. Charts are old: ICU4C 3.8 versus glibc 2.12.3 and ICU4C 4.8 versus glibc 2.13 (about 2008 to 2011); both libraries have changed since. The chart page itself warns results vary with hardware and compiler and that strcoll is sensitive to code alignment (10% swings). The benchmark code is public (icu4c/source/test/perf/collationperf/collperf.cpp in unicode-org/icu, which 'compar[es] collation performance and key lengths of ICU, Windows native collation and Unix/POSIX collation') but no committed results were found. A second snippet-only claim: a PostgreSQL mailing-list message reports ICU normalization at 0.861 s and 0.651 s against PostgreSQL's built-in 4.024 s and 6.655 s on two conversions (hardware and method unknown). The guessed baseline 'standard UTF-8 processing' does not match any evidence; this is a collation and normalization claim. ICU is also the incumbent that other Unicode libraries benchmark against.
